query: I am interested in high-entropy alloys for extreme temperature applications. How can we predict melting properties such as the melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity for multi-component systems where experimental data is sparse or unreliable due to high melting points? I am looking for a hypothesis on a computational methodology that balances accuracy with the need to screen vast compositional spaces, along with prior evidence on why standard approaches struggle in this regime and what a valid boundary condition for such a method would be.

generation.hypothesis: To predict melting properties (Tm, ΔSfus, Cp) for multi-component refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) where experimental data is sparse, a hybrid computational methodology combining the CALPHAD (Calculation of Phase Diagrams) approach with machine learning (ML) potentials derived from first-principles (DFT) calculations is required. Standard CALPHAD struggles in this regime because thermodynamic databases for refractory elements (W, Mo, Ta, Nb, V) in complex multi-principal configurations are often incomplete or extrapolated, leading to high uncertainty in the liquid phase description. The proposed method involves: 1) Using DFT to calculate the enthalpy of formation and vibrational free energy for a representative set of RHEA compositions (e.g., W-Mo-Ta-Nb-V systems) to parameterize the liquid phase model in CALPHAD. 2) Training a Machine Learning model on these DFT-CALPHAD hybrid data points to rapidly predict the Gibbs energy of the liquid and solid phases across the vast compositional space. 3) Applying the Gibbs energy minimization to determine Tm and ΔSfus. The boundary condition for this method is that the alloy system must form a stable single-phase solid solution (BCC) or a predictable two-phase mixture at high temperatures, as the method relies on the validity of the thermodynamic models for the liquid and solid phases. If the system exhibits strong chemical ordering or complex intermetallic formation that deviates significantly from the training set, the prediction uncertainty increases.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-principal element refractory alloy system (e.g., W-Mo-Ta-Nb-V) in a hypothetical liquid or solid state, with no prior experimental melting data.
generation.intervention: Perform high-throughput DFT calculations on a subset of compositions to generate thermodynamic descriptors (enthalpy of mixing, vibrational entropy) and train a Machine Learning model to interpolate/extrapolate these properties across the full compositional space. Integrate these ML-predicted parameters into a CALPHAD framework to compute phase equilibria and melting properties.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 2000 K to 4000 K (typical for RHEAs); Pressure: 1 atm; Compositional space: 5-7 principal elements with concentrations between 10-40 at.%. Computational resources: High-performance computing (HPC) with parallelization to handle the scaling of the number of components.
generation.structural_mediator: Configurational entropy of mixing and lattice distortion effects in the BCC solid solution, which stabilize the solid phase and influence the entropy of fusion. The liquid phase is modeled as a disordered solution with specific interaction parameters derived from DFT.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism relies on the CALPHAD method's ability to model phase equilibria by minimizing Gibbs free energy. Since standard databases lack accurate liquid phase parameters for complex RHEAs, the mechanism is augmented by deriving these parameters from first-principles DFT calculations (which accurately capture electronic and vibrational contributions to free energy) and using Machine Learning to bridge the gap between the limited DFT data and the vast compositional space. This hybrid approach overcomes the 'black box' nature of pure ML and the 'incomplete database' limitation of pure CALPHAD. The prediction of Tm is derived from the intersection of the solid and liquid Gibbs energy curves, while ΔSfus is the difference in entropy at this temperature. Cp is derived from the temperature derivative of the enthalpy.
generation.predicted_outcome: A computational workflow capable of predicting Tm within ±50 K and ΔSfus within ±10% for RHEAs with 5-7 components, with a computational cost reduction of >90% compared to pure DFT-based phase diagram calculations. The method will identify compositions with Tm > 2500 K and high ΔSfus, suitable for extreme temperature applications.
generation.baseline: Standard CALPHAD calculations using existing thermodynamic databases, which often yield large errors (>100 K) for Tm in complex RHEAs due to missing or inaccurate liquid phase parameters for refractory multi-component systems.
generation.boundary: The method is valid for systems that form solid solutions or predictable two-phase mixtures at high temperatures. It may fail for systems with complex, unstable intermetallic phases or strong chemical ordering that are not captured by the training set of DFT calculations. The method assumes the liquid phase can be adequately modeled as a disordered solution.
generation.uncertainty: High uncertainty in the prediction of Tm for compositions far from the DFT training set (extrapolation). The accuracy of the ML model depends on the diversity and quality of the DFT data. The assumption of a disordered liquid phase may introduce errors if short-range order persists in the melt.

falsification_experiment.design: Select three RHEA compositions (e.g., W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20, W15Mo15Ta20Nb20V30, and a new quinary system) that have been synthesized and for which melting points have been measured experimentally (or can be measured via high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry). Run the proposed hybrid CALPHAD-ML workflow to predict their Tm and ΔSfus.
measurements: Melting temperature (Tm) via DSC or laser melting point measurement
Entropy of fusion (ΔSfus) via calorimetry or derived from Tm and enthalpy of fusion
Microstructural verification of phase stability at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted Tm deviates from the experimental Tm by more than ±100 K for any of the three test compositions, or if the predicted ΔSfus deviates by more than ±20%, the hypothesis that the hybrid CALPHAD-ML method provides accurate predictions for this class of alloys is falsified. Additionally, if the method fails to predict the correct phase stability (e.g., predicts a single phase where a two-phase mixture is observed), it is falsified.

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
